title: The gold ring and the filthy coat
hookLine: who gets the good seat? James, Jesus' guest list, and a love of preference for the poor
carry: a preferential love for the poor

lines: A GOLD RING, A FILTHY COAT.
cards: Two visitors come through the door of the meeting at the same moment. One wears a gold ring and fine clothes. The other wears a filthy coat.
Someone hurries over to the first and says, in the old King James words, "Sit thou here in a good place." To the second: "Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool."
That scene is in the letter of James, and James asks his readers straight out whether they've started sorting people by their clothes.
Underneath sits a plain question that any gathering answers, whether it means to or not: who gets the good seat?

teach.h: CALL THE POOR TO THE FEAST.
teach.b: Jesus answers the seat question at a dinner party in Luke's Gospel. Watching guests elbow toward the best places, he turns to the host with advice for next time: "call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind."
And the reason: "for they cannot recompense thee." A guest list built on who can invite you back is a trade. A guest list that starts with the poor is a gift.
Catholic teaching gives this a name, often called the preferential option for the poor; the Catholic catechism speaks of the poor as the object of the Church's preferential love.

It doesn't mean God loves rich people less, or that being poor makes anyone holy. It means that when choices get made, about money, time, laws or who sits where, the needs of the poor are weighed first.
Other churches arrive there by their own roads.
John Wesley, the Anglican preacher behind the Methodist movement, preached a sermon on visiting the sick, pressing his hearers to go in person, not only to send help.
Sending help is good, he said, but going yourself teaches what sending can't. You meet the people themselves: their faces, their names, what their week is actually like.

teach.h: FIRST MEANS TIME AND A NAME.
teach.b: So "first" turns out to be practical: the good seat, the top of the budget, and on an ordinary Tuesday, an hour given to someone who can't pay it back.

how: Christians live this out through church food pantries, shelters and visiting ministries; Catholic social teaching names it the preferential option for the poor, and Methodist and other churches teach personal visiting alongside giving.

James describes that scene to challenge it: the congregation had started sorting people by their clothes.
Jesus told a host to invite the poor because they can't repay
"for they cannot recompense thee" (Luke 14:14). a guest list built on repayment is a trade; this one is a gift.
the preferential option for the poor means God loves the rich less
in Catholic teaching it means the needs of the poor are weighed first when choices are made, not that anyone is loved less.

games.q: you're greeting people at the door. a man with a gold ring and a man in a filthy coat walk in together, and there's one good seat left. what do you do?
o: give the good seat to the man with the ring.
give the good seat to the man in the filthy coat.
point them both to the back and let them sort it out.
games.why: James condemns giving the good place to the rich and sending the poor to stand, and Jesus tells hosts to call the poor first. the text's answer is the man in the filthy coat.

practice: Bring to mind one person you know, or pass often, who is struggling to get by: a neighbor between jobs, a relative behind on rent, the man on the same corner every morning.

Notice whether you know their name, and let them sit in the front row of your mind for a while, ahead of your own errands. If you pray, you can hold them before God, by name, or by face if you don't know the name.

wordCard.voice: The poor first. When choices are made about money, time or a seat at the table, the needs of the poor are weighed before anyone else's.

orig.note: Greek: poor, often in the sense of a beggar; the word used in James 2 and Luke 14.

carryVoice: Your line: a preferential love for the poor. First means the seat, the budget and your time. See you tomorrow.
